title.text: Decisions, repeats and functions: if, for, and a tested function

objects.text: How do we make Python decide and repeat, so we never copy a formula down thousands of rows?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 6 of 24  |  Module B: Python for data
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session you stored values and read error messages. So far your code has run straight down the page. Today it learns to decide with if, to repeat with for, and to reuse steps in a function. You already do all three in a spreadsheet, with IF, fill down and a formula you name.

We write each one in Python beside its spreadsheet cousin, on one real rule: the Lakeside Mart loyalty tiers.

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can make Python decide, with if, elif and else, and you can build the tests that go inside them from comparison and logical operators. You can repeat steps with a for loop and keep a running total with an accumulator. You can wrap steps in a function with a parameter and a return value.

And you can test that function at its edge cases with assert, and trace code by hand to find a fault. We build one real rule, the Lakeside Mart loyalty tiers.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts first,
then a Python notebook lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_83d54561.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Pictures and plain words first. Then you open the notebook. Then the tests and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 5 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with laptops closed. After a ten minute break you open a Colab notebook for a forty-five minute lab, where you write the loyalty tier function, test it at its edges, and use it on six customers.

The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  An error ends with: NameError: name 'price' is not defined. Which line do you read first, and what does it tell you?
2.  What does '3200' + '8400' give in Python, and why?
3.  A list and a dictionary both hold several values. How do you find one value in each?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 5. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. An error ends with: NameError: name 'price' is not defined. Which line do you read first, and what does it tell you?

A good answer is this. The last line. Python has nothing stored under the name price: check the spelling, or run the cell that creates it.

Question two. What does '3200' + '8400' give in Python, and why?

A good answer is this. '32008400'. Both values are strings, so plus joins them. Convert them with int() first to add.

Question three. A list and a dictionary both hold several values. How do you find one value in each?

A good answer is this. In a list by its index, counting from 0. In a dictionary by its key.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Code that runs one branch, chosen by a test that is True or False. It is the IF function written as code.

Repeating the same steps for each item in a list. It is fill down written as code.
A named set of steps. The parameter is the name for the value that comes in, the argument is the value you pass, and the return value is the answer.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Conditional statement (if, elif, else). Code that runs one branch, chosen by a test that is True or False. It is the IF function written as code.

Boolean expression. A test that gives True or False, built with comparison operators such as >= and logical operators such as and.

Iteration (for loop). Repeating the same steps for each item in a list. It is fill down written as code.

Function (parameter, argument, return value). A named set of steps. The parameter is the name for the value that comes in, the argument is the value you pass, and the return value is the answer.

Edge case (boundary value) and test case. An edge case sits exactly where a rule changes. A test case pairs an input with the output you expect.

title.text:
The rule we will code: the
Lakeside Mart loyalty tiers

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_person_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_coin_0.39.png

objects.text: 1 point for every UGX 1,000 spent. Source: loyalty_programme.txt, one of the Lakeside Mart policy files.

slides.notes:
Here is the rule we code today. It comes from the Lakeside Mart loyalty programme policy. A customer who gives a phone number joins as Basic and earns one point for every thousand shillings spent. Silver starts at two thousand points in twelve months, and Gold at six thousand.

The last column turns points into shillings: two million for Silver, six million for Gold. Keep those two numbers in mind. They are the boundaries where the rule changes, and the places where a function most often goes wrong. How would you write this rule as nested IFs in Excel?

title.text:
A conditional statement chooses one branch:
Python takes the first test that is True

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_flowchart_7.70x4.80_f3e85e6a.png
objects.alt: A conditional statement chooses one branch: Python takes the first test that is True

objects.text: Conditional statement: if, elif and else.

runs.text: Tests run from the top. The first True branch runs.
elif means else if. else catches the rest.
The indent shows which lines belong to which test.

slides.notes:
In Excel you decide with the IF function, and a third tier means one IF inside another. Python writes the same decision as a conditional statement: if, then elif, short for else if, then else. The flowchart follows a customer with 2,450 points. The first test, 6,000 or more, is False, so Python moves down.

The second test, 2,000 or more, is True, so the answer is Silver and Python skips the rest. The order matters, because the first True branch wins. The indented lines belong to the test above them. Which test must come first if you swapped them?

title.text:
A Boolean expression is a test that gives True
or False, built with comparison operators

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_pin_0.38.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.38.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_clock_0.38.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_tag_0.38.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.38.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.38.png

objects.text: One equals sign stores a value. The comparison equal to is two equals signs. Excel uses one for both jobs.

slides.notes:
A Boolean expression is a test that gives True or False, named after the mathematician George Boole. You build one with a comparison operator. Two equals signs ask whether two values are equal, where Excel uses a single sign. Not equal is exclamation mark equals, where Excel writes less than, greater than.

The other four are the comparisons you know. With 2,450 points, the table shows each result, computed by Python. Notice that greater than or equal to 2,000 is True, and greater than 2,450 is False. Which of these would catch someone who spent exactly the boundary?

title.text:
Logical operators and, or and not
combine tests, like AND and OR in Excel

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_logic_7.70x4.80_1b4a4e36.png
objects.alt: Logical operators and, or and not combine tests, like AND and OR in Excel

objects.text: Logical operators: and, or, not.

runs.text: and is True only when both tests are True.
2,450 points: A and B is True. 6,000 points: it is False.
or needs one True. not flips True and False.

slides.notes:
Logical operators combine tests. The picture draws two tests along the points axis. Test A, 2,000 or more, is True from 2,000 upwards. Test B, below 6,000, is True up to 6,000. A and B is True only where both bars overlap, which is the gold band, and that is exactly the Silver tier.

With 2,450 points it is True. With exactly 6,000 points it is False, because 6,000 is not below 6,000. Or is True when at least one test is True, and not flips the answer. Excel has AND, OR and NOT for the same jobs. What would A or B give for 7,000 points?

title.text: Read the recipe: if, elif and else decide a tier

objects.text: 2450 points is Silver
In plain words

runs.text: The first test is False, so Python skips Gold.
The second test is True, so tier becomes Silver.
The indent and the colon mark each branch.
print runs once, whichever branch ran.

slides.notes:
Read the recipe aloud with me. Points is stored as 2,450. The first test asks whether it is 6,000 or more. It is False, so the Gold line is skipped. The elif asks whether it is 2,000 or more. That is True, so tier becomes Silver, and Python skips the else.

Notice the colon at the end of each test and the indent under it. They are part of the grammar. The last line, at the left edge, runs once whichever branch was taken. The output was produced by running this exact code here: 2450 points is Silver. What would print if points were 1,999?

title.text:
A for loop repeats the same steps for
each item, like fill down in a sheet

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_loop_7.70x4.80_1b3d7f75.png
objects.alt: A for loop repeats the same steps for each item, like fill down in a sheet

objects.text: Iteration: repeating steps for each item.

runs.text: The for line takes one item at a time.
The indented lines run once per item.
// keeps the whole part: one point per UGX 1,000.

slides.notes:
In a spreadsheet you write a formula once and drag it down the column. That is fill down. Python does the same with a for loop, which is a form of iteration, repeating steps for each item in a list. On the left is the column of spend, with the formula INT of A2 over a thousand filled down.

On the right, the for line takes one spend at a time, and the indented line works out its points. The double slash keeps the whole part, so 46,660 shillings gives 46 points. Five items or five thousand, the code stays the same. Why is that better than dragging a formula down?

title.text: Read the recipe: a loop over five customer spends

objects.text:
46660 UGX is 46 points
2388850 UGX is 2388 points
82700 UGX is 82 points
2757805 UGX is 2757 points
26650 UGX is 26 points
In plain words

runs.text: spends is a list of five 2025 totals from orders.csv.
The loop takes one spend at a time.
The indented lines run once for each item.
print shows the spend and its points.

slides.notes:
Here is the loop on real numbers. These five totals are the 2025 order totals of five Lakeside customers, computed from orders dot csv. The loop takes one spend at a time, works out the points, and prints a line. So 46,660 gives 46 points, and 2,388,850 gives 2,388.

Nothing here decides a tier yet. Next we add a function that does. These totals are small because orders dot csv is a five percent sample of till transactions, so real spending is much higher. What would you change to print the tier instead of the points?

title.text:
An accumulator builds a running total
inside a loop, like SUM or a running balance

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_trace_11.90x4.25_6c0f24d4.png
objects.alt: An accumulator builds a running total inside a loop, like SUM or a running balance

objects.text: Customer C1322 placed three orders in 2025. The accumulator ends at 2,388,850 UGX.

slides.notes:
This is a trace table. It follows the code one pass at a time. Customer C1322 made three orders in 2025. Before the loop, total starts at zero. That variable is the accumulator, a variable that collects a result as the loop goes round. Pass one adds 2,289,600.

Pass two adds 63,300. Pass three adds 35,950, and the total is 2,388,850. The pattern is always the same: start at zero, then total equals total plus value. Python also has a sum function, but the accumulator is the idea behind it. What would the accumulator start at if you wanted the largest value?

title.text:
A function is a named set of steps: a parameter
goes in and a return value comes out

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_function_7.70x4.80_4c0c3e00.png
objects.alt: A function is a named set of steps: a parameter goes in and a return value comes out

objects.text: Function: a formula you name yourself.

runs.text: Parameter: the name for the value that comes in.
Argument: the value you pass when you call it.
return sends the value back to the caller.

slides.notes:
A function is a formula you name yourself. This one is called loyalty points. The def line gives the name and one parameter, spend ugx, which is the name for the value that comes in. The line in triple quotes is the docstring, a short note on what the function does.

The indented lines are the body, and return sends the answer back. To use it you call it with an argument. Here the argument is 2,388,850, and the return value is 2388. The parameter is the name inside the function, and the argument is the actual value. Why is a docstring useful for a colleague?

title.text: Read the recipe: the loyalty_tier function

objects.text:
Silver
Basic
In plain words

runs.text: def, the name and the parameter spend_ugx.
The docstring says what it does.
The body works out points, then tests Gold first.
Two calls: 2,388,850 gives Silver, 46,660 gives Basic.

slides.notes:
Here is the whole rule as one function. The def line names it and its parameter. The docstring says what it returns. The body turns spend into points with a double slash, then tests Gold first, Silver second, and Basic for everyone left. Each branch uses return, which sends the tier back to whoever called the function.

The two calls at the bottom were run here. 2,388,850 shillings gives Silver, and 46,660 shillings gives Basic. Notice that the function does not print. It returns. Why might returning be more useful than printing?

title.text:
Write the function once, then
call it for every customer

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_081df9a1.png
objects.alt: Write the function once, then call it for every customer

objects.text: A loop repeats the work. A function holds the rule. Together they answer the question for six customers or six million.

slides.notes:
Now we put the loop and the function together. First an accumulator in a loop builds each customer total. Then a loop goes through the customers one at a time. For each one it calls loyalty tier, the single tested rule, and gets a tier back. Finally we count how many customers fall in each tier.

The rule lives in one place. If the policy moves Silver to two thousand five hundred points, you change one line in one function and every result updates. How would that change work in a sheet with the IF copied in many cells?

title.text:
An edge case (boundary value) sits
exactly where the rule changes

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_numline_11.90x4.25_2b355f54.png
objects.alt: An edge case (boundary value) sits exactly where the rule changes

objects.text: Off-by-one error: writing > where the rule needs >=. Only the boundary value exposes it.

slides.notes:
An edge case, also called a boundary value, is an input exactly where a rule changes. The picture marks the two boundaries of our rule. At two million shillings the tier changes from Basic to Silver, and at six million from Silver to Gold. Bugs hide here. If someone writes greater than where the rule needs greater than or equal to, the function passes every ordinary value and fails only the value exactly on the line.

That slip has a name, the off-by-one error. So test the value just below each boundary and the value exactly on it. Which value would you test for a boundary of 5,000?

title.text:
A test case pairs an input with the
expected output, and it passes or fails

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_tests_11.90x4.25_4cab59ee.png
objects.alt: A test case pairs an input with the expected output, and it passes or fails

objects.text: Expected comes from the policy. Got is what the function returned.

slides.notes:
A test case is one input paired with the output you expect, worked out by hand from the policy before you run anything. The table has five test cases for our function: zero spend, one shilling below Silver, exactly Silver, one shilling below Gold, and exactly Gold. Each one compares the expected tier with what the function returned.

All five pass. A small set of tests like this for one function is called a set of unit tests. Writing the expected column first, from the policy, is what makes the test honest. Why must the expected column come from the policy and not from the code?

title.text:
Read the recipe: assert stops with
an AssertionError when a test fails

objects.text: All 5 tests pass
In plain words

runs.text: assert checks that a test is True.
If it is True, Python carries on silently.
If it is False, Python stops with an AssertionError.
The last line prints only if all five passed.

slides.notes:
The assert statement is how you run a test in code. It says: this must be True. If it is True, Python carries on without a word. If it is False, Python stops with an AssertionError, and the notebook shows you which line failed. Here are our five test cases written as asserts.

Nothing appears until the last line, which prints that all five tests pass. That silence is the good news. If I assert that the buggy version returns Gold for six million, Python stops and the last line of the error is an AssertionError. What does silence from an assert tell you?

title.text:
Trace code by hand to find a fault:
tier_v1 tests Silver before Gold

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_trace_11.90x4.25_c4261fc1.png
objects.alt: Trace code by hand to find a fault: tier_v1 tests Silver before Gold

objects.text: A colleague's tier_v1 returns Silver for 7,500,000 UGX. The correct tier is Gold.

slides.notes:
Reading and tracing someone else's code is a daily job. Here is a colleague's function, tier v1. Trace it with 7,500,000 shillings. Line two stores 7,500 points. Line three asks whether 7,500 is 2,000 or more. It is True, so line four returns Silver and the function ends.

The Gold test on line five is never reached. So a customer who spent seven and a half million is called Silver. The fault lies in the order of the branches, and every number in the code is correct. Tracing with one value by hand found it in four steps.

What is the rule for ordering the branches?

title.text:
The same test cases catch
the fault: tier_v1 fails 1 of 5

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_c_tests_11.90x4.25_bd9a1b76.png
objects.alt: The same test cases catch the fault: tier_v1 fails 1 of 5

objects.text: A failed test shows the input, the expected output and the actual output.

slides.notes:
Run the same five test cases against tier v1, and the fault shows up at once. one of the five test cases fails, and the failing row tells you the input, the expected output and what the function actually returned. Only the exact Gold boundary case fails, because the Silver test catches everything above two million first.

That points straight at the order of the branches. This is why you write test cases before you trust a function, and why you keep them afterwards: if someone edits the function next year, the tests tell them at once whether it still works. Which of the five test cases found the fault first?

title.text:
Four common mistakes, and the
message Python gives for each

rows.text: SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Maybe you meant '==' or ':=' instead of '='?
A function with no return line
Add return, so the caller gets the value.
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for //: 'str' and 'int'
Remove the commas and convert with int().
An if with nothing indented under it
IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement on line 2
Indent the lines that belong to the if.

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_0.50.png

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: Lines under a def, if or for are not indented.
Indent the body by four spaces.
The function prints a tier, but the result is None
The function has no return line.
Use return, not print, inside the function.
A check says NOT YET for the edge cases
The test uses > where the rule needs >=.
The function returned a different tier than expected.
Read the failing line, trace that one input by hand.
Clean the commas, then use int().

slides.notes:
Five messages you may meet. An IndentationError means the lines under def, if or for are not indented. A function that prints but returns None has no return line. A check that says NOT YET for the edge cases usually means a greater than where the rule needs greater than or equal to.

An AssertionError means the function returned a different tier than you expected, so trace that single input by hand. And a TypeError on the double slash means the spend is a string. Read the last line first. It usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: What is the tier for exactly 6,000,000 UGX, and why is it a good test case?
Gold. It is an edge case: exactly on the boundary, where a greater than slip would give Silver.
What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
The parameter is the name inside the function, such as spend_ugx. The argument is the value you pass, such as 2,388,850.
An accumulator holds 0 before the loop. What does it hold after the pass over each of three orders?
It holds the running total: the first order, then the first two together, then all three.
